Why Is Everything Red?

▼ Market update

The market had a big sell-off: investors sold shares in lots of different kinds of companies, not just tech.

1🤖Worries about AI

Big tech companies are spending huge amounts on AI. Investors wonder: will it pay off?

2🏦Worries about interest rates

Prices keep going up, and nobody is sure what the Federal Reserve will do next. Higher rates make borrowing cost more, and people may spend less.

3😬Worry spreads

When investors get nervous, they sell lots of stocks at once, even very different businesses.

Nov 17 All 11 parts of the stock market went down. For every stock that went up, more than 5 went down.
Stock Market Challenge · market update
Why is everything red?2:30–4:30
  • Ask first: “Why do you think almost every stock fell?” Take two or three guesses, then click to reveal the reasons one at a time.
  • Keep the words simple. “Sell-off” = lots of people selling at the same time. “Interest rate” = the extra cost of borrowing money.
  • The last click shows the Nov 17 fact: all 11 sectors of the S&P 500 fell, and decliners beat gainers more than 5 to 1.
  • Ticker badges show each stock’s change since Week 4, from the price board data.

Are They All Bad Businesses Now?

If Microsoft, Nike, Disney, and Roblox all drop on the same day, does that mean they’re all suddenly bad businesses?

MicrosoftStill makes Windows, Xbox, and software used all over the world.
NikeStill sells shoes and sports gear all over the world.
DisneyStill makes movies, runs theme parks, and streams Disney+.
RobloxStill played by millions of kids every day.
Hands up: Yes? No? Not sure?

Not necessarily! These companies didn’t change overnight. Investors just feel less sure about the economy and about what companies will earn in the future.

Stock prices don’t just show how companies are doing today. They also show what investors believe will happen tomorrow.

Why Do Stock Prices Move?

Week 4 (Nov 11) → Week 5 (Nov 17)

Idea 1Expectations matter

Nike is still one of the biggest sports brands in the world. But investors expected faster growth, so its stock has struggled this year. This week it shared its plan for the future at a big investor meeting.

Idea 2News matters

Millions of kids still play Roblox. This year it lowered its sales forecast, and governments are asking tougher questions about keeping kids safe online. News like that can move a stock fast.

Idea 3The whole market matters

UnitedHealth recently reported better results than expected. But when worried investors pushed the whole market down three days in a row, it slipped too.

A stock can fall even when the company is still successful. Investors watch expectations, news, and the whole market.

  • Slides 4–5 covered why the whole market fell. Here, go fast: one company per idea.
  • Nike: Investor Day was Nov 17, its first in almost ten years. The stock is down about a third over the past year because growth kept disappointing.
  • Roblox: it cut its 2026 bookings outlook, and child-safety rules are a risk.
  • UnitedHealth: it beat expectations in Q3, but the S&P 500 fell three sessions in a row through Nov 16.
  • Change percentages come from the Week 4 and Week 5 snapshots, not single-day moves.

Innovation: Make It Better

Innovation isn’t always inventing something brand new. Sometimes it means making something that already exists better.

Exhibit A: The Bad Backpack

What’s wrong with this backpack?

1One giant pocket. Pencils and erasers sink to the bottom and get lost.
2Skinny straps. A heavy load digs into your shoulders.
3Water bottle rides inside. When it leaks, your books get soaked.
4No safe spot for homework. Papers get crumpled or lost.
5Thin fabric. Rain and dirt soak right in.

Every problem is a chance to innovate.

Innovation: make it better
Find the problems22:00–25:00
  • Read the quote. Ask: “Can you think of something that got better without being brand new?” (phones, sneakers, cars)
  • Show the bad backpack. Ask: “What’s wrong with this backpack?” Let students point things out first.
  • Then click to reveal each problem. Its number lights up on the drawing.
  • Ask: “Has this ever happened to you?” Real problems are where good improvements start.

Backpack 2.0: How We Make It Better

Backpack 2.0
1Organizer pockets + pen loopsFixes: lost supplies
2Wide padded straps + chest clipFixes: sore shoulders (spreads the weight)
3Bottle pocket on the outsideFixes: soaked books
4Stiff homework folder sleeveFixes: crumpled homework
5Waterproof fabricFixes: rain and dirt soaking in
?Built-in light-up speakerCool… but it adds weight and cost, needs charging, and doesn’t fix a real problem.

Good innovation fixes problems people care about. More features isn’t automatically better. Which fix would you pay extra for?

Innovation: make it better
Make it better25:00–30:00
  • Before each click, ask: “How would you fix problem #1?” Take an idea or two, then reveal the fix. Its number lights up on the drawing.
  • Before / After swaps the drawings so students can compare.
  • The last card is a trap: ask “Is this a good improvement?” before revealing why not.
  • Close: “Which fix would you pay extra for?” Then connect it: “Next, you’ll do this with Phone Box.”

Would Anyone Buy It?

A good invention

Works, and solves the problem.

A successful business

People choose it, use it, and pay for it.

  • 🙋Would you personally use Phone Box 2.0?
  • 👪Would your parents buy it?
  • 💲How much would someone reasonably pay?
  • 🤷What happens if nobody wants the product?
Would anyone buy it?
Invention vs. business55:00–58:00
  • Read the two boxes. Ask: “Can something be a great invention and still be a bad business?”
  • Reveal the questions one at a time and take a few answers for each.
  • Price: just collect a few guesses out loud. Costs, pricing, and market research come in a later lesson.

Make It Better: The Big Idea

A great invention solves a problem.

A great business solves a problem people care enough about to pay for.
